etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English administren, from Old French aminister, from Latin administrare (“to manage, execute”), from ad (“to”) + ministrare (“to attend, serve”), from minister (“servant”); see minister.

quote.citation: 1708, [John Philips], “Book I”, in Cyder. […], London:  […]  J[acob] Tonson, […], →OCLC, page 3:
quote.text: [Let zephyrs] administer their tepid, genial airs.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: Justice was administered between man and man with an exactness and purity not before known.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To manage or supervise the conduct, performance or execution of; to govern or regulate the parameters for the conduct, performance or execution of; to work in an administrative capacity.

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], epistle 3, London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: For forms of government let fools contest: / Whate'er is best administered is best.

quote.citation: 2006, Rongxing Guo, Territorial Disputes and Resource Management: A Global Handbook‎[1], →ISBN, →OCLC, page 224:
quote.text: Located in the northwestern side of the Black Sea, Snake Island, or called ostriv Zmiyinyy in Ukrainian and Insula Serpilor in Romanian, is currently administered by Ukraine but claimed by Romania.

quote.citation: 1712 September 17 (Gregorian calendar), [Joseph Addison], “SATURDAY, September 6, 1712”, in The Spectator, number 477; republished in Alexander Chalmers, editor, The Spectator; a New Edition, […], volume V, New York, N.Y.: D[aniel] Appleton & Company, 1853, →OCLC:
quote.text: A fountain  […]  administers to the pleasure as well as the plenty of the place.The spelling has been modernized.

definitions.definition: (law) To settle, as the estate of one who dies without a will, or whose will fails of an executor.

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: Swear  […]  to keep the oath that we administer.

definitions.definition: (transitive, medicine) To give (a drug, to a patient), be it orally or by any other means.
(transitive, medicine) To cause (a patient, human or animal) to ingest (a drug), either by openly offering or through deceit.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter XV, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: A noxious drug had been administered to him.
